newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia, Indonesia sign historic maritime treaty.
newsitem.headline: Australia, Indonesia sign historic maritime treaty.

text.p: Australia and Indonesia signed a long-awaited sea boundary treaty on Friday, establishing exclusive economic zones between the two Asia-Pacific nations after some 30 years of negotiations.
"Once it enters into force, the treaty will be of economic benefit to both countries," Australian and Indonesian foreign ministers said in a joint statement after signing the treaty.
"The finalisation of the seabed boundary provides a basis on which exploitation of natural resources can proceed in a climate of confidence and certainty," they said.
The sea boundary is 3,000 kms (1,840 miles) long and extends from Australia's Northern Territory in the east to beyond Australia's Christmas Island in the Indian Ocean.
But it does not affect the 1989 Timor Gap Treaty which covers exploitation mainly of oil and gas reserves in the Timor Sea between Timor island and Australia.
The Timor Gap Treaty went into effect in 1991 and has a lifespan of 40 years.
The sea boundary treaty is the first major bilateral international treaty to be signed by Australia's conservative government since it came to power in March last year.
"It's fair, it's equitable, it's in Australia's national interests," said Foreign Minister Alexander Downer.
Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas said the treaty reflected a strong bilateral relationship, despite past spats over trade and human rights.
"There have occurred many events that in one way or another have caused tension in the relations between our two countries," Alatas told reporters.

"Yet our relations remain broadly...stable because of the very same spirit of mutual respect and partnership which motivated our two countries to assiduously negotiate these maritime boundaries issues," he said.
Relations between Indonesia and Australia have been rocky at times, with Jakarta angered by critical reporting of its policies, particularly over human rights and East Timor.

Australia is the only Western nation to recognise Indonesia's sovereignty over East Timor, which it invaded in 1975. The United Nations has so far refused to recognise Jakarta's 1976 annexation of the former Portuguese colony.
A small group of protesters staged a demonstration in Perth on Friday against the treaty, claiming Australia was appeasing Indonesia over East Timor by signing the agreement.

"The Australian people...will be outraged when our foreign minister panders to (Indonesian foreign minister) Alatas while the ongoing gross human rights violations occur inside occupied East Timor," the Friends of East Timor said in a statement.

While the new treaty does not affect the Timor oil treaty, which allows Canberra and Jakarta to jointly exploit oil and gas reserves off East Timor, Australia said it did finalise a water boundary halfway between Australia and East Timor.

Asked if it was legal to draw a boundary between a territory that the United Nations does not recognise is part of Indonesia, a foreign affairs official said: "Our view is that it is internationally acceptable".
